newsitem.title: USA: Rebel advances spur U.S. call for change in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rebel advances spur U.S. call for change in Zaire.

text.p: Rapid rebel advances across Zaire are lending increasing urgency to U.S. appeals for a transitional government and elections to head off the disintegration of the vast African nation.
For weeks, U.S. officials have been saying privately that ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, Washington's one-time anti-communist ally, is "irrelevant" to Zaire's future.
This week, as Laurent Kabila's rebels captured the key cities of Mbuji-Mayi and Lubumbashi, officials went public with what came close to calls for Mobutu to quit.

"Mobutuism is about to become a creature of history, because the support for President Mobutu is not sufficient to lead Zaire into the next chapter of its history," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said on Wednesday.

This was a final step away from the man that Washington once backed as a bulwark against communism both in his own country and when the United States was trying to unseat the Soviet-backed government in neighbouring Angola in the 1970s.

Mobutu lost importance for Washington with the end of the Cold War. After providing some $2 billion in aid for him over the years, the Americans cut off all military and economic assistance by 1994 as their focus switched to establishing a multi-party democracy in Zaire.

Since Kabila's uprising erupted last October in eastern Zaire, Washington has repeatedly called for a ceasefire, peace talks and "transitional arrangements" leading to elections which in theory are supposed to be held by July.

The point was repeated on Wednesday by State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns. "What we are seeking is an orderly transition to democracy through elections. That is the only way to ensure stability," he told a briefing.
Privately, however, officials conceded that Kabila's incentive to negotiate was declining the more territory his forces captured.
Negotiations between the Zaire government and the rebels ended inconclusively in South Africa on Tuesday. On Wednesday the rebels said there would be no ceasefire until Mobutu resigned.

Although the Pentagon's top Africa expert, Vincent Kern, told a Congressional hearing on Tuesday that "we have no strategic interests in Zaire," U.S. officials say the enormous and mineral-rich country is still of major importance.

"The fact is that Zaire is one of the most important countries in Africa," Burns said. "There is no question about that, given its geopolitical location, given its economy, given the fact that it borders on nine countries.

"Whatever happens in Zaire inevitably is going to affect what happens in central Africa and in southern Africa, and the stability of nations bordering Zaire will be affected by how this political transition, how this civil war ends."

The main American fear is that Zaire could split up as a result of the war. The South Africa talks produced agreement to maintain Zaire's territorial integrity, but Burns said this "modest progress" had not stopped the situation deteriorating.

Chaos in the heart of Africa and a continuing refugee problem could revive unwelcome demands for the United States to take part in a multinational intervention force, something Washington has successfully evaded so far.
Coupled with this is uncertainty about what Kabila might do should the whole of Zaire fall into his hands on his own terms.

U.S. officials have not forgotten that the veteran Zairean rebel once associated with Latin American revolutionary Che Guevara and said the possibility of him establishing a leftist regime remained at least "a concern" for U.S. policymakers.
The officials also express concern at reports of massacres in areas taken over by Kabila's forces.
One official said that Kabila had recently "made some very good soundings on the democracy front". But he added, "At this point he's very much an enigma".
